title: HybridRAG: A Fusion of Graph and Vector Retrieval  - Mitesh Patel, NVIDIA

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is HybridRAG architecture combining knowledge graphs and vector databases for retrieval, directly matching retrieval_search_knowledge inclusion criteria for RAG architecture as the main subject. The talk presents a knowledge-base retrieval system applicable across multiple verticals including retail, finance, and enterprise employee data. The talk covers system development (triplet extraction, vector DB, knowledge graph creation), evaluation (Ragas, Nemotron 340B), and optimization (LoRA fine-tuning, data cleaning, cuGraph acceleration). Prerequisites include RAG, vector databases, embeddings, and knowledge graph traversal familiarity, indicating an intermediate level. A 20-minute conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair with code demonstrations available on GitHub. The talk includes practical demonstrations, quantitative accuracy improvements from 71% to 87%, and real NVIDIA tool integrations from a developer advocate.

summary: Mitesh Patel, leading NVIDIA's developer advocate team, presents HybridRAG—a fusion of GraphRAG and VectorRAG designed to overcome conventional RAG limitations in capturing nuanced entity relationships from complex documents. Knowledge graphs represent networks of relationships between entities through triplets (entity-relationship-entity2), offering more detailed capture of connections than semantic approaches alone. The system architecture comprises four components: data, data processing, graph/vector database creation, and inferencing, with offline (one-time data processing) and online (querying and response generation) phases. Semantic vector database creation is straightforward—documents are chunked with overlap for context preservation, embedded, and stored. Knowledge graph creation requires significantly more effort, using LLMs with carefully defined ontologies via prompt engineering to extract structured triplets. Patel emphasizes spending approximately 80% of development time refining ontologies, as noisy triplets lead to noisy retrieval. Multi-hop graph traversal is stressed over single-hop retrieval, but deeper hops increase latency. NVIDIA's cuGraph library accelerates graph searches and integrates with NetworkX. For evaluation, Patel introduces the Ragas library for end-to-end RAG assessment across faithfulness, answer relevancy, precision, recall, and other metrics, with flexibility to use custom LLMs. He also highlights NVIDIA's Nemotron 340B reward model for evaluating LLM responses. Patel shares the 80/20 rule: building a graph RAG system takes 20% of time, but optimizing it takes 80%. Key optimization strategies include data cleaning (removing apostrophes, brackets, unnecessary characters), reducing longer outputs, and LoRA fine-tuning of Llama 3.1, which improved triplet extraction accuracy from 71% to 87% on 100 documents. For deciding between graph, semantic, or hybrid approaches, Patel advises considering data structure (well-structured data like retail, FSI, and employee databases suit graph systems), the feasibility of creating a good knowledge graph from unstructured data, and whether the use case requires understanding complex relationships, noting that graph systems are compute-heavy. All demonstration notebooks, including fine-tuning code, are available on GitHub, and a two-hour workshop covers the material in depth.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Mitesh Patel introduces himself as leader of NVIDIA's developer advocate team, which creates technical workflows and notebooks released on GitHub. He outlines the talk's focus on creating a graph RAG system with hybrid capabilities, developed with partners and NVIDIA colleagues.

sections.title: Knowledge Graph Fundamentals
sections.summary: Patel explains knowledge graphs as networks representing relationships between entities (people, places, concepts, events). He gives an example of his relationship to the AI Engineer conference as a speaker. Knowledge graphs capture entity relationships in more detail than semantic RAG, providing comprehensive knowledge views and organizing data from multiple sources.

sections.title: HybridRAG Architecture
sections.summary: The system comprises four components: data, data processing, graph/vector database creation, and inferencing. The pipeline splits into offline (one-time data processing) and online (querying and response generation) phases. The top portion builds the semantic vector database; the bottom creates the knowledge graph, which requires more careful steps.

sections.title: Knowledge Graph Creation: Triplets and Ontology
sections.summary: Patel demonstrates triplet extraction from unstructured documents using an Exxon Mobil quarterly results example. LLMs with prompt engineering extract ontology-specific triplets. He emphasizes spending ~80% of development time refining ontologies, as noisy triplets produce noisy retrieval. This iterative process is critical to knowledge graph quality.

sections.title: Semantic Vector Database Creation
sections.summary: Vector database creation is straightforward: documents are chunked with overlap to preserve context between adjacent chunks. Embedding models convert chunks into vectors. Patel notes that vector databases do not exploit entity relationships—a key advantage of graph RAG.

sections.title: Retrieval: Multi-Hop Strategies and Acceleration
sections.summary: Retrieval requires multi-hop graph traversal to exploit relationships across multiple nodes. Deeper hops provide better context but increase latency, requiring a sweet spot. NVIDIA's cuGraph library accelerates graph searches, enabling deeper exploration while reducing latency, and integrates with NetworkX.

sections.title: Evaluation with Ragas and Nemotron Reward Model
sections.summary: Patel introduces the Ragas library for end-to-end RAG evaluation, covering faithfulness, answer relevancy, precision, recall, helpfulness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Ragas evaluates queries, retrieval, and responses separately, and offers flexibility to use custom LLMs via API rather than only its default GPT. He also highlights NVIDIA's Nemotron 340B, a 340 billion parameter reward model trained to evaluate and judge responses of other LLMs across five parameters.

sections.title: Optimization: The 80/20 Rule and Improvement Strategies
sections.summary: Patel applies the 80/20 rule: building a graph RAG system takes 20% of time, but optimizing it takes 80%. He shares optimization strategies including data cleaning (removing apostrophes, brackets, unnecessary characters), reducing longer outputs, and LoRA fine-tuning of Llama models. Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 improved triplet extraction accuracy from 71% to 87% on 100 documents. He cautions that accuracy on small document sets may not scale to larger pools, but relative improvement holds.

sections.title: Latency and cuGraph Performance at Scale
sections.summary: As graphs grow to millions or billions of nodes, search latency becomes critical. cuGraph, available through NetworkX as a pip-installable library, provides GPU acceleration. Performance tests show drastic latency reduction in graph search algorithms, enabling practical deployment at scale.

sections.title: Choosing Graph vs Semantic vs Hybrid
sections.summary: Patel provides a decision framework: it depends on data structure and use case. Well-structured data (retail, FSI, employee databases) suits graph-based systems. For unstructured data, consider whether a good knowledge graph can be created. Graph systems are compute-heavy, so they only make sense when the use case requires understanding complex relationships.

sections.title: Resources and Conclusion
sections.summary: All code, including Llama 3.1 LoRA fine-tuning notebooks, is available on GitHub. A two-hour workshop covers the material in depth. Patel encourages joining NVIDIA developer programs and mailing lists for updates. He will be available at the Neo4j booth for further questions.
